findings.rationale: event_assignments() emits an assignment for every event in the domain on every generated action, setting each flag to true only when that action emitted it and false otherwise (a one-hot reset). Because every action re-applies this reset, two distinct events' flags can never be true at the same time unless a single action emits both. saga_guards() joins step.awaits with ' and ' when awaits_mode == "all", producing a guard such as (event_E1 and event_E2) that is unsatisfiable whenever the awaited events are produced by different actions (separate observe actions or commands). Those saga steps therefore never fire, silently breaking the documented 'all' await semantics.

render_saga_actions() emits saga observe actions with no 'requires' precondition, unlike the guarded step and compensation actions. Each observe action body calls event_assignments(), which resets every non-observed event flag to false. The observe entry point is thus unguarded and repeatable: a duplicate or later delivery of the observed event re-runs the global flag reset, clearing flags that other in-flight saga steps are awaiting and silently disabling those steps.

normalize() rewrites enum member comparisons using String::replace on the patterns '{variable} == {member}' and '{variable} != {member}', and rewrites membership lists by locating the marker '{variable} in [' with str::find; neither enforces identifier word boundaries (unlike replace_identifier(), which checks the surrounding bytes). When one field name is a suffix of another identifier in the expression (e.g. variable 'x' with text 'max in [1, 2]'), the match begins mid-token and replace_range/replace corrupts the generated condition into invalid or semantically wrong source (e.g. 'ma(x == 1 or x == 2)').

normalize() resolves a variable's type with an exact-name lookup self.ty(ty) where ty is the fully rendered type. This matches only bare enum types, so for compound types such as Option<OrderStatus> the lookup returns None and both the '==/!=' member substitution and the enum mapping inside 'in [...]' are skipped. Conditions on Option-wrapped enum fields therefore retain raw member names instead of the canonical enum values, diverging from how bare enums are normalized.
